docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This subsystem monitors soil saturation levels using an analog soil moisture sensor. A Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller reads the sensor’s analog output, processes the data, and transmits the results to the main system for further analysis and control actions.

Power is supplied by a 9V, 3A wall adapter, which is regulated down to 5V, 1.5A through a voltage regulator to provide stable and safe operation for both the microcontroller and sensor.

docs.title: Sensors and Interfaces
docs.text:
Connected Sensor: Analog Soil Moisture Sensor

System Interface: Communicates soil data to other subsystems (e.g., motor control or irrigation logic) through an 8-pin connector, enabling coordinated system responses based on soil conditions.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Subsystem board powered from 9 V input through a 5 V regulator. Includes a PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano microcontroller connected to: - Analog soil moisture sensor - Temperature / humidity sensor - Rain sensor - 8-pin connector to communicate with other boards

docs.title: Soil Moisture Sensors
docs.text:
Table 1: Soil Moisture Sensor Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: SEN0114 Soil Moisture Sensor Module$2.70 — eachlink to product Simple analog outputLow costCompact design Corrodes over time if left in soilRequires calibration for accuracy Option 2: ST0160 Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor V2.0$8.60 — eachlink to product No corrosion (capacitive)Stable analog readingsLow power consumption More expensive than SEN0114Slightly larger PCB footprint Option 3: Industrial Soil Moisture & Temperature Sensor$79 — eachlink to product Industrial-grade durabilityIncludes temperature outputLong-term outdoor reliability Higher costRequires analog-to-current interface circuitry

Choice: Option 2 — ST0160 Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor V2.0

Rationale: Provides much more corrosion-free sensing with stable analog output and is good for long-term moisture monitoring in outdoor environments while maintaining low cost and simple integration with the PIC ADC.

docs.title: Temperature & Humidity Sensors
docs.text:
Table 2: Temperature & Humidity Sensor Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: DHT22 / AM2302 Sensor$9.39 — eachlink to product Low costSimple one-wire interfaceGood community support Slow sampling rateLimited accuracy (±0.5 °C, ±2 % RH) Option 2: Adafruit Sensirion SHT31-D Sensor (I²C)$13.95 — eachlink to product High accuracy (±0.3 °C, ±2 % RH)I²C communicationFast response time Moderate costRequires I²C pins on MCU Option 3: SHT45 Precision Temperature Humidity Module$14.99 — eachlink to product Very high precision (±0.1 °C, ±1 % RH)Low power consumptionCompact form factor Higher priceMay require fine-pitch connector or adapter

Choice: Option 2 — Adafruit Sensirion SHT31-D Sensor

Rationale: Offers a balance between precision, power efficiency, and integration simplicity using I²C communication working well with the PIC18F16Q41’s peripheral support.

docs.title: Rain Water Sensors
docs.text:
Table 3: Rain Sensor Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: ST0247 Raindrop Detection Sensor Module$8.60 — eachlink to product Low cost and easy to interfaceAnalog and digital outputs Susceptible to corrosion and false positivesNot quantitative Option 2: SEN0545 Rain Sensor (UART Output)$22.68 — eachlink to product Digital UART interfaceCorrosion-resistant coatingStable signal processing built-in Slightly higher costRequires UART parsing logic Option 3: Optical Rain Gauge Sensor (RS485 Pulse Output)$85.72 — eachlink to product Industrial precision and long lifetimeNon-contact optical detection High priceRequires RS485 interface and external housing

Choice: Option 2 — SEN0545 Rain Sensor (UART Output)

Rationale: Provides reliable digital output with minimal maintenance and better environmental resistance than basic analog boards and avoiding the complexity and cost of industrial RS485 systems.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
Table 4: Voltage Regulator Comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: LM7805 Linear Regulator$0.64 — eachlink to product Simple designLow noiseStable 5 V output Inefficient when dropping 9 V to 5 VGenerates heat at higher currents Option 2: UA78L05ACLP $1.69 — eachlink to product Compact packageLow quiescent currentPerfect for ≤ 100 mA loads Limited output current (100 mA max)Not ideal for high-current systems

Choice: Option 1 — LM7805 Linear Regulator

Rationale: System current is moderate so the LM7805 offers sufficient efficiency with low noise, needed for stable analog measurements on the sensor inputs.

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
Component: PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano Supply: 5 V from LM7805 Regulator

Rationale: Used for its low-power operation, built-in ADC channels for analog sensor inputs, I²C and UART support for digital sensors, and fast development and debugging.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is designed to support the Smart Irrigation Subsystem Board. It regulates a 9 V input down to 5 V using an LM7805 linear regulator with diode and fuse protection. The 5 V rail powers a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller that monitors soil moisture (ST0160 via MCP6004 op-amp), temperature/humidity (SHT31-D via I²C), and rainfall (SEN0545 via UART). The system provides stable sensor inputs, onboard filtering, and a ribbon connector for inter-board communication.”

Figure 1: Showing the sensors, microcontroller, and power delivery schematic.

docs.text:
Team Number: 101 Project Name: Smart Irrigation Subsystem Board Team Member Names: Liam, Isaiah, and Raj Version: 1.0

docs.title: Section A – All Major Components
docs.text:
Component Name Part / Example Supply Voltage (V) Qty. Abs. Max Current (mA) Total Current (mA) Microcontroller (Curiosity Nano) PIC18F16Q41 Curiosity Nano 5 1 500 500 Soil Moisture Sensor ST0160 Capacitive 5 1 5 5 Temperature / Humidity Sensor SHT31-D 5 1 2 2 Rain Sensor SEN0545 (UART) 5 1 40 40 Subtotal 547mA

Arithmetic: 500 + 5 + 2 + 40 = 547mA total subsystem current

docs.title: Section B – Power Rails
docs.text:
+5V Rail - Subtotal = 547 mA - Safety margin (25%) = 547 × 1.25 = 683.75mA → round to 684mA

Arithmetic: 547 × 1.25 = (547 × 5) / 4 = 2735 / 4 = 683.75mA

docs.title: Section C – Regulator Selection
docs.text:
Regulator Option Input Range (V) Max Output (mA) Pros Cons LM7805 (linear) 7 – 25V 1500 Simple, low noise, handles high current Inefficient (9V → 5V drop causes heat under load; may need heat sink) UA78L05ACLP (TO-92, 100 mA max) 7 – 35V 100 Compact, simple, low quiescent current Limited to 100mA output (too low for this system)

Choice: LM7805 Linear Regulator

Rationale: With the total estimated current of 684mA (including the 25% margin), the LM7805 provides sufficient current capacity and thermal headroom. The UA78L05ACLP’s 100mA limit is below system requirements.

Regulator heat / dissipation check: Voltage drop = 9V − 5V = 4V Load current = 684mA = 0.684A Power dissipated = 4V × 0.684A = 2.736W

Result: LM7805 will require a small heat sink at this power level.

docs.title: Section D – External Power Source
docs.text:
Power Source Example Output Voltage (V) Max Current (mA) Wall Adapter Generic 9V DC Adapter 9 3000
  • Required on +5V rail (with 25% margin): 684mA
  • Remaining capacity: 3000 − 684 = 2316 mA

Arithmetic: 1500 − 684 = 816mA remaining capacity before voltage Regulator Failure

Battery option: 3000 mAh Li-ion battery This is not used in the design but if it was:

Battery life = 3000 mAh / 50 mA = 60 hours (≈2.5 days) Reducing average current to 50 mA using sleep + duty cycling for maximum battery life.

Result: Battery operation is not practical due to a higher current draw.
